questions.knowledge_point: Parametrizing Part of a Horizontal Hyperbola
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058380/assets/a2f0f570ecc68de1a5b34fb3bd1b341fc83a728b026b035dde848dbf986e441b.png)

The quarter-hyperbola above is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-hyperbola, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058380/assets/e7ef7fd90c828767359daf69f68f406d61e3f82ad86b1f6b3a9480c99dedadf8.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0],$ we get the quarter-hyperbola.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe the required quarter-hyperbola are

$$
x=3\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},0].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given Graphically
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058380/assets/999d1d14a31f9619306efe6b1c2ebc6e900a52bf4e2d2edd7230e7dd7c9b25b9.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm 2x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(\pm a,0).$ From the graph, we have that $(1,0)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=1.$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y=\pm 2x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{2}{1} \\ \frac{b}{1} & =\frac{2}{1} \\ b & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{2\sqrt{3}} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{3})^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{12} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{12} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{12}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
